name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MATCHING_Q01 - Match alkane synthesis reactions with characteristic reagents

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Method / Reaction) List II (Reagent / Reaction Condition)
(A) Wurtz reaction (I) Sodium salt of carboxylic acid heated with soda lime
(B) Kolbe's electrolytic method (II) Alkyl halide treated with sodium metal in dry ether
(C) Decarboxylation (III) Aqueous solution of sodium or potassium carboxylate electrolysed at the anode
(D) Catalytic hydrogenation (IV) Alkene or alkyne treated with dihydrogen in presence of platinum, palladium, or nickel

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Principle of the Wurtz reaction
Alkyl halides on treatment with sodium metal in dry ethereal solution give higher alkanes containing an even number of carbon atoms through carbon-carbon bond coupling. Therefore, the Wurtz reaction corresponds to alkyl halide treated with sodium metal in dry ether.

Step 2: Principle of Kolbe's electrolytic method
An aqueous solution of sodium or potassium salt of a carboxylic acid on electrolysis undergoes anodic oxidation of carboxylate ions, forming alkyl free radicals that dimerize to yield alkanes containing an even number of carbon atoms at the anode. Therefore, Kolbe's electrolytic method corresponds to aqueous solution of sodium or potassium carboxylate electrolysed at the anode.

Step 3: Principle of decarboxylation
Sodium salts of carboxylic acids, when heated with soda lime (a mixture of sodium hydroxide and calcium oxide, \(\mathrm{NaOH} + \mathrm{CaO}\)), undergo elimination of carbon dioxide to yield an alkane possessing one carbon atom less than the parent carboxylic acid. Therefore, decarboxylation corresponds to sodium salt of carboxylic acid heated with soda lime.

Step 4: Principle of catalytic hydrogenation
Dihydrogen gas adds across the multiple bonds of unsaturated hydrocarbons (alkenes and alkynes) on the active surface of finely divided transition metal catalysts such as platinum, palladium, or nickel to yield the corresponding saturated alkanes. Therefore, catalytic hydrogenation corresponds to alkene or alkyne treated with dihydrogen in presence of platinum, palladium, or nickel.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Combining these individual reaction descriptions establishes the correct set of pairings: Wurtz reaction pairs with alkyl halide treated with sodium metal in dry ether; Kolbe's electrolytic method pairs with aqueous solution of sodium or potassium carboxylate electrolysed at the anode; Decarboxylation pairs with sodium salt of carboxylic acid heated with soda lime; and Catalytic hydrogenation pairs with alkene or alkyne treated with dihydrogen in presence of platinum, palladium, or nickel.
Final Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MATCHING_Q02 - Match ethane conformational parameters with their values

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Conformational Parameter of Ethane) List II (Value / Physical Concept)
(A) Dihedral angle in eclipsed ethane (I) \(60^\circ\)
(B) Dihedral angle in staggered ethane (II) \(0^\circ\)
(C) Energy difference between eclipsed and staggered forms (III) Torsional strain
(D) Repulsive interaction between adjacent bond electron clouds (IV) \(12.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the eclipsed conformation
In the eclipsed conformation of ethane, the hydrogen atoms attached to the two carbon atoms are aligned as close together as possible along the carbon-carbon axis. The angle of rotation about the carbon-carbon bond (dihedral angle) between adjacent carbon-hydrogen bonds is precisely \(0^\circ\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the staggered conformation
In the staggered conformation of ethane, the carbon-hydrogen bonds on adjacent carbons are as far apart in space as possible. The dihedral angle between adjacent front and rear carbon-hydrogen bonds is \(60^\circ\).

Step 3: Evaluation of the torsional energy barrier
The energy difference between the higher-energy eclipsed extreme and the lower-energy staggered extreme of ethane is of the order of \(12.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), representing the small rotational energy barrier that intermolecular collisions easily overcome at room temperature.

Step 4: Identification of the repulsive force
The repulsive interaction arising between the electron clouds of adjacent carbon-hydrogen sigma bonds when they approach one another during rotation around the carbon-carbon single bond is defined as torsional strain.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
The resulting relationships are: Dihedral angle in eclipsed ethane is \(0^\circ\); Dihedral angle in staggered ethane is \(60^\circ\); Energy difference between eclipsed and staggered forms is \(12.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\); and Repulsive interaction between adjacent bond electron clouds is torsional strain.
Final Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MATCHING_Q03 - Match controlled oxidation conditions of alkanes with products

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Oxidation Reaction) List II (Major Product)
(A) \(2\mathrm{CH}_4 + \mathrm{O}_2 \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Cu}/523\text{ K}/100\text{ atm}}\) (I) Methanal
(B) \(\mathrm{CH}_4 + \mathrm{O}_2 \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{Mo}_2\mathrm{O}_3}\) (II) Ethanoic acid
(C) \(2\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_3 + 3\mathrm{O}_2 \xrightarrow[\Delta]{(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COO})_2\mathrm{Mn}}\) (III) Methanol
(D) \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{CH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KMnO}_4}\) (IV) 2-Methylpropan-2-ol

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Controlled catalytic oxidation of methane over copper
Methane heated with dioxygen at \(523\text{ K}\) and \(100\text{ atm}\) in the presence of a copper tube catalyst undergoes partial oxidation to yield methanol according to the equation:
\[2\mathrm{CH}_4 + \mathrm{O}_2 \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Cu}/523\text{ K}/100\text{ atm}} 2\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{OH}\]

Step 2: Catalytic oxidation of methane over molybdenum oxide
Methane heated with air or dioxygen in the presence of molybdenum oxide (\(\mathrm{Mo}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) catalyst is selectively oxidized to an aldehyde, methanal, according to the equation:
\[\mathrm{CH}_4 + \mathrm{O}_2 \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{Mo}_2\mathrm{O}_3} \mathrm{HCHO} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]

Step 3: Catalytic oxidation of ethane using manganese acetate
Ethane on controlled oxidation with air in the presence of manganese(II) acetate, \((\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COO})_2\mathrm{Mn}\), yields a carboxylic acid, ethanoic acid, according to the equation:
\[2\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_3 + 3\mathrm{O}_2 \xrightarrow[\Delta]{(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COO})_2\mathrm{Mn}} 2\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]

Step 4: Oxidation of branched alkane containing a tertiary hydrogen
Alkanes generally resist oxidation by potassium permanganate; however, an alkane bearing a tertiary hydrogen atom, such as 2-methylpropane (isobutane), is readily oxidized by \(\mathrm{KMnO}_4\) to the corresponding tertiary alcohol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butyl alcohol):
\[(\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{CH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KMnO}_4} (\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{COH}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
The specific reagents and resulting products correlate as: Reaction with copper catalyst yields methanol; Reaction with molybdenum oxide catalyst yields methanal; Reaction with manganese acetate catalyst yields ethanoic acid; and Reaction of isobutane with potassium permanganate yields 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
Final Answer: (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MATCHING_Q04 - Match alkene addition reagents with their principal products

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Reaction of Propene with Reagent) List II (Major Organic Product)
(A) Reaction with cold, dilute aqueous \(\mathrm{KMnO}_4\) (Baeyer's reagent) (I) 2-Bromopropane
(B) Reaction with \(\mathrm{HBr}\) in the presence of benzoyl peroxide (II) 1-Bromopropane
(C) Reaction with \(\mathrm{HBr}\) in the absence of peroxide (III) Propane-1,2-diol
(D) Ozonolysis followed by cleavage with \(\mathrm{Zn}/\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (IV) Ethanal and methanal

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Hydroxylation by Baeyer's reagent
Alkenes react with cold, dilute, aqueous solution of potassium permanganate (Baeyer's reagent) at \(273\text{ K}\) to undergo syn-dihydroxylation, yielding vicinal glycols. Propene (\(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}_2\)) produces propane-1,2-diol.

Step 2: Free radical addition in the presence of peroxide
In the presence of an organic peroxide, the addition of hydrogen bromide to an unsymmetrical alkene proceeds via a free-radical chain mechanism (peroxide effect or Kharasch effect). Bromine free radical attacks the terminal carbon to form the more stable secondary free radical, yielding 1-bromopropane as the major anti-Markovnikov product.

Step 3: Electrophilic addition according to Markovnikov's rule
In the absence of peroxides, addition of hydrogen bromide proceeds via an electrophilic addition mechanism involving carbocation intermediates. Protonation yields the more stable secondary carbocation (\(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}^+-\mathrm{CH}_3\)), which combines with bromide ion to form 2-bromopropane as the major product.

Step 4: Reductive ozonolysis of an unsymmetrical terminal alkene
Addition of ozone across the double bond of propene forms propene ozonide. Reductive cleavage of this ozonide by zinc dust and water cleaves the double bond into smaller carbonyl compounds, yielding ethanal (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHO}\)) and methanal (\(\mathrm{HCHO}\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
The correct mappings are: Reaction with Baeyer's reagent gives propane-1,2-diol; Addition of \(\mathrm{HBr}\) with peroxide gives 1-bromopropane; Addition of \(\mathrm{HBr}\) without peroxide gives 2-bromopropane; and Ozonolysis gives ethanal and methanal.
Final Answer: (A)-(III), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MATCHING_Q05 - Match reactions of alkynes with resulting organic products

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Reaction of Alkynes) List II (Product / Characteristic Result)
(A) Ethyne passed through red hot iron tube at \(873\text{ K}\) (I) Propanone
(B) Hydration of propyne with dilute \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) and \(\mathrm{HgSO}_4\) at \(333\text{ K}\) (II) Benzene
(C) Treatment of ethyne with sodamide (\(\mathrm{NaNH}_2\)) (III) 1,1-Dibromoethane
(D) Addition of two moles of \(\mathrm{HBr}\) to ethyne (IV) Sodium ethynide and ammonia

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Cyclic polymerization of ethyne
Passing ethyne gas through a red-hot iron tube maintained at \(873\text{ K}\) induces cyclic trimerization of three ethyne molecules to produce the aromatic hydrocarbon benzene (\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6\)).

Step 2: Mercuric ion-catalysed hydration of an alkyne
Addition of water to propyne in the presence of mercuric sulphate (\(\mathrm{HgSO}_4\)) and dilute sulphuric acid (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\)) at \(333\text{ K}\) follows Markovnikov's rule to give an enol intermediate, prop-1-en-2-ol. Rapid tautomerization (keto-enol isomerism) converts this enol into propanone (acetone).

Step 3: Acidic character of terminal alkynes
The hydrogen atoms attached to sp-hybridized triply bonded carbon atoms have significant s-character (\(50\%\)) and high electronegativity, making them acidic. When treated with the strong base sodamide (\(\mathrm{NaNH}_2\)), ethyne donates a proton to form sodium ethynide with the liberation of ammonia gas (\(\mathrm{NH}_3\)).

Step 4: Hydrohalogenation of ethyne to gem-dihalide
Ethyne adds one molecule of hydrogen bromide to form bromoethene. Addition of the second molecule of hydrogen bromide occurs across the double bond in accordance with Markovnikov's rule to attach the second bromine atom to the carbon already bearing bromine, producing the geminal dihalide 1,1-dibromoethane (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHBr}_2\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
The matched relationships are: Passing ethyne through red hot iron tube at \(873\text{ K}\) gives benzene; Hydration of propyne gives propanone; Treatment of ethyne with sodamide gives sodium ethynide and ammonia; and Addition of two moles of \(\mathrm{HBr}\) to ethyne gives 1,1-dibromoethane.
Final Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MATCHING_Q06 - Match electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions with attacking electrophiles

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Electrophilic Substitution of Benzene) List II (Active Electrophile Involved)
(A) Nitration with concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) and concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) (I) Chloronium ion (\(\mathrm{Cl}^+\))
(B) Chlorination with \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\) and anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\) (II) Acylium ion (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{C}^+\mathrm{O}\))
(C) Friedel-Crafts acylation with acetyl chloride and anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\) (III) Nitronium ion (\(\mathrm{NO}_2^+\))
(D) Sulphonation with fuming sulphuric acid (oleum) (IV) Neutral sulphur trioxide (\(\mathrm{SO}_3\))

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Electrophile in aromatic nitration
In the nitration of benzene, concentrated sulphuric acid acts as a Brønsted acid and protonates nitric acid. Subsequent elimination of water generates the active electrophile, the nitronium ion (\(\mathrm{NO}_2^+\)):
\[\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 + \mathrm{HNO}_3 \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{HSO}_4^- + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}^+-\mathrm{NO}_2 \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NO}_2^+ + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{HSO}_4^-\]

Step 2: Electrophile in aromatic halogenation
During chlorination, the Lewis acid catalyst anhydrous aluminium chloride (\(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\)) polarizes and cleaves the chlorine molecule by accepting a chloride ion, generating the chloronium ion electrophile (\(\mathrm{Cl}^+\)):
\[\mathrm{Cl}-\mathrm{Cl} + \mathrm{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl}^+ + [\mathrm{AlCl}_4]^-\]

Step 3: Electrophile in Friedel-Crafts acylation
Reaction of an acyl halide such as acetyl chloride with anhydrous aluminium chloride leads to abstraction of chloride by the Lewis acid to generate the resonance-stabilized acylium ion (\(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{C}^+=\mathrm{O} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{C}\equiv\mathrm{O}^+\)):
\[\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COCl} + \mathrm{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{C}^+\mathrm{O} + [\mathrm{AlCl}_4]^-\]

Step 4: Electrophile in sulphonation
Sulphonation is carried out using fuming sulphuric acid containing dissolved sulphur trioxide. In this medium, the strong electrophile is the neutral electrophilic molecule sulphur trioxide (\(\mathrm{SO}_3\)), in which the highly electronegative oxygen atoms render the central sulphur atom strongly electron-deficient.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
The reactions matched with their respective electrophiles are: Nitration involves nitronium ion; Chlorination involves chloronium ion; Friedel-Crafts acylation involves acylium ion; and Sulphonation involves neutral sulphur trioxide.
Final Answer: (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MATCHING_Q07 - Match benzene ring substituents with directive and activating effects

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Substituent on Benzene Ring) List II (Electronic Nature and Directive Influence)
(A) \(-\mathrm{OH}\) (I) Strongly deactivating and meta-directing
(B) \(-\mathrm{NO}_2\) (II) Strongly activating and ortho/para-directing
(C) \(-\mathrm{Cl}\) (III) Moderately deactivating and ortho/para-directing
(D) \(-\mathrm{CH}_3\) (IV) Activating and ortho/para-directing

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Directive effect and activation by the phenolic hydroxyl group
The \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group exhibits a negative inductive effect (\(-I\)) but a much stronger positive resonance effect (\(+R\)) due to the delocalization of the oxygen lone pair into the ring. This greatly increases the electron density at the ortho- and para-positions relative to the meta-position, making the group strongly activating and ortho/para-directing.

Step 2: Directive effect and deactivation by the nitro group
The \(-\mathrm{NO}_2\) group is strongly electron-withdrawing both by a powerful negative inductive effect (\(-I\)) and a strong negative resonance effect (\(-R\)). It reduces electron density throughout the ring, particularly at the ortho- and para-positions, rendering the ring strongly deactivated and directing electrophiles to the comparatively less electron-depleted meta-position.

Step 3: Anomalous effect of halogen substituents
In aryl halides such as chlorobenzene, chlorine has a strong electron-withdrawing inductive effect (\(-I\)) that outweighs its weak resonance electron donation (\(+R\)), decreasing the net electron density of the ring and making it moderately deactivating. However, resonance delocalization selectively places partial negative charges at the ortho- and para-positions, making halogens ortho/para-directing.

Step 4: Directive effect of an alkyl substituent
An alkyl group such as \(-\mathrm{CH}_3\) donates electron density into the aromatic ring via inductive effect (\(+I\)) and hyperconjugation. This increases electron density preferentially at the ortho- and para-positions, rendering the methyl group activating and ortho/para-directing.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Matching each substituent with its behavior yields: The hydroxyl group is strongly activating and ortho/para-directing; The nitro group is strongly deactivating and meta-directing; The chloro group is moderately deactivating and ortho/para-directing; and The methyl group is activating and ortho/para-directing.
Final Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MATCHING_Q08 - Match aromatic species with their pi electron counts

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II according to Hückel's rule of aromaticity (\((4n + 2)\pi\) electrons):

List I (Aromatic Species) List II (Hückel Integer \(n\) and \(\pi\)-Electron Count)
(A) Cyclopentadienyl anion (I) \(n = 2\) with \(10\pi\) electrons
(B) Cycloheptatrienyl cation (II) \(n = 1\) with \(6\pi\) electrons in a five-membered ring
(C) Naphthalene (III) \(n = 3\) with \(14\pi\) electrons
(D) Anthracene (IV) \(n = 1\) with \(6\pi\) electrons in a seven-membered ring

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Application of Hückel's rule to cyclopentadienyl anion
Cyclopentadienyl anion contains two conjugated carbon-carbon double bonds (\(4\pi\) electrons) and a non-bonding lone pair of electrons on the negatively charged carbon (\(2\pi\) electrons) fully delocalized over a planar 5-membered ring. The total number of \(\pi\) electrons is \(6\), satisfying the Hückel formula \(4n + 2 = 6\) with \(n = 1\).

Step 2: Application of Hückel's rule to cycloheptatrienyl cation
Cycloheptatrienyl cation (tropylium ion) has three conjugated carbon-carbon double bonds (\(6\pi\) electrons) and a vacant p-orbital on the positively charged carbon. The \(6\pi\) electrons are completely delocalized over the planar 7-membered ring, corresponding to \(4n + 2 = 6\) with \(n = 1\).

Step 3: Application of Hückel's rule to naphthalene
Naphthalene is a bicyclic aromatic hydrocarbon with two fused benzene rings. It has five conjugated double bonds providing a total of \(10\pi\) electrons fully delocalized across the planar framework, satisfying \(4n + 2 = 10\) with \(n = 2\).

Step 4: Application of Hückel's rule to anthracene
Anthracene is a tricyclic benzenoid hydrocarbon possessing three linearly fused benzene rings. It contains seven conjugated double bonds comprising \(14\pi\) electrons delocalized over the planar ring system, satisfying \(4n + 2 = 14\) with \(n = 3\).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Comparing the species with the electronic parameters: Cyclopentadienyl anion has \(n = 1\) with \(6\pi\) electrons in a five-membered ring; Cycloheptatrienyl cation has \(n = 1\) with \(6\pi\) electrons in a seven-membered ring; Naphthalene has \(n = 2\) with \(10\pi\) electrons; and Anthracene has \(n = 3\) with \(14\pi\) electrons.
Final Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MATCHING_Q09 - Match alkenes with their respective ozonolysis cleavage products

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Alkene Subjected to Ozonolysis with \(\mathrm{Zn}/\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) List II (Carbonyl Products Formed)
(A) But-2-ene (I) Propan-2-one and methanal
(B) 2-Methylprop-1-ene (II) Two moles of ethanal
(C) Propene (III) Ethanal and propanal
(D) Pent-2-ene (IV) Ethanal and methanal

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Cleavage of symmetrical but-2-ene
The structure of but-2-ene is \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_3\). Ozonolysis cleaves the carbon-carbon double bond, converting each \(=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_3\) fragment into an aldehyde molecule, \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHO}\). Hence, two moles of ethanal are produced.

Step 2: Cleavage of branched 2-methylprop-1-ene
The structure of 2-methylprop-1-ene is \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{CH}_2\). Cleavage of the double bond transforms the disubstituted carbon fragment \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\mathrm{C}=\) into a ketone, propan-2-one (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COCH}_3\)), and the terminal \(=\mathrm{CH}_2\) fragment into an aldehyde, methanal (\(\mathrm{HCHO}\)).

Step 3: Cleavage of propene
The structure of propene is \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}_2\). Ozonolysis cleaves the double bond into two carbonyl fragments: the \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\) portion becomes ethanal (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHO}\)) and the \(=\mathrm{CH}_2\) portion becomes methanal (\(\mathrm{HCHO}\)).

Step 4: Cleavage of unsymmetrical pent-2-ene
The structure of pent-2-ene is \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\). Oxidative cleavage of the double bond yields an ethanal molecule from the two-carbon side (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHO}\)) and a propanal molecule from the three-carbon side (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CHO}\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
The resulting cleavage products match as: But-2-ene yields two moles of ethanal; 2-Methylprop-1-ene yields propan-2-one and methanal; Propene yields ethanal and methanal; and Pent-2-ene yields ethanal and propanal.
Final Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MATCHING_Q10 - Match aromatic hydrocarbons with their ring system structures

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Polynuclear Aromatic Hydrocarbon) List II (Structural Characteristic)
(A) 1,2-Benzanthracene (I) Two fused benzene rings (\(10\pi\) electrons)
(B) 1,2,5,6-Dibenzanthracene (II) Three angularly fused benzene rings (\(14\pi\) electrons)
(C) Naphthalene (III) Four fused benzene rings (carcinogenic hydrocarbon)
(D) Phenanthrene (IV) Five fused benzene rings (carcinogenic hydrocarbon)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural identification of 1,2-benzanthracene
1,2-Benzanthracene consists of an anthracene core (three linearly fused benzene rings) fused with an additional benzene ring at positions 1 and 2. It contains a total of four fused benzene rings and is recognized as a potent carcinogenic polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbon.

Step 2: Structural identification of 1,2,5,6-dibenzanthracene
1,2,5,6-Dibenzanthracene consists of an anthracene nucleus fused to two additional benzene rings at positions 1,2 and 5,6. It possesses a total of five fused benzene rings and is cited as an important carcinogenic polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon.

Step 3: Structural identification of naphthalene
Naphthalene is the simplest bicyclic benzenoid aromatic hydrocarbon, consisting of two benzene rings fused together in an ortho arrangement with a shared carbon-carbon bond, containing \(10\pi\) electrons.

Step 4: Structural identification of phenanthrene
Phenanthrene is an angular tricyclic benzenoid hydrocarbon composed of three fused benzene rings arranged in an angular (non-linear) orientation, containing \(14\pi\) electrons.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Correlating each hydrocarbon with its ring configuration: 1,2-Benzanthracene corresponds to four fused benzene rings; 1,2,5,6-Dibenzanthracene corresponds to five fused benzene rings; Naphthalene corresponds to two fused benzene rings (\(10\pi\) electrons); and Phenanthrene corresponds to three angularly fused benzene rings (\(14\pi\) electrons).
Final Answer: (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
